content.thinking:
I'm thinking through the module import path, since the task specifies importing from "agentic-3js-builder" rather than relative paths, and I can't fully verify typechecking will resolve it but I'll proceed with that convention.

For the design itself, I'm sketching a whimsical capybara roughly 1.1m long and 0.5m tall with a chubby barrel body, blocky head, big snout, tiny ears, and a serene closed-eye face, plus a small round bird perched on its head with a blue back and orange belly, both with little blush cheek details to keep the whimsy factor high.

Now I'm working out the skeleton: hips root around [0,0.36,-0.2] with a spine chain running from rump to chest to neck to head, quadruped-style with short ~0.2 length legs and a barrel radius near 0.25, mapping out coordinates for the spine curve, neck, and blocky head/snout geometry before setting up the joint chains and parenting for the rig.

I'm sorting out how catmull-rom path points map to joint names and spans, trying to figure out where the rump bone should sit relative to hips so the body loft covers the area behind the hips joint without creating a zero-length bone.

Defining the body radius function...

Setting up the spine chain as spine1/spine2/spine3 feeding into the head joint, angled slightly forward and down. For the head itself I'm building a blocky capybara skull with a big square muzzle, upper and lower jaw pieces, a dark nose pad with nostrils, small high-set eyes, and tiny rounded ears tucked near the back.

Working out the skull position and ellipsoid proportions, then shaping the snout as a blunt frustum box angled forward with flat caps to keep that blocky capybara look, oriented so widths run along X and height runs up. Now setting up a separate lower jaw joint to attach the chin piece.

Positioning the jaw box beneath the snout, slightly narrower and recessed so it tucks under and stays hidden where it overlaps, leaving just enough showing to form a visible lower lip line. Considering whether to add a thin dark slit or a decal for the mouth to give the face a subtle, serene smile.

For the actual face details, I'll decal a nose pad with nostril slits and a philtrum onto the flat front face of the snout, then curve smile lines out to the sides, plus pink blush ellipses decaled onto the cheeks from either side for a whimsical touch.

For the eyes, I'm debating between sparkly big whimsical eyes versus the smaller, sleepier eyes real capybaras have—landing on medium-sized dark eyes with highlights and a droopy brown lid line to keep it friendly but still recognizably capybara-like.

I'll place the eye decals using the skull surface's azimuth/elevation projection from the skull center, positioning them symmetrically at roughly ±50° azimuth and 18° elevation, no mirroring needed since the drawings themselves are symmetric. Then I'm figuring out where the bird perches on top of the head, with the skull top sitting around y≈0.60.

Now I'm designing the bird itself: a round body sphere, small head, cone beak, capsule wings, fan tail, and tiny orange legs attached to the head joint so it moves naturally with head motion. I'm giving it a whimsical turquoise-and-cream color scheme with an orange beak, a three-feather crest, glossy eye decals, rosy cheeks, and considering small extras like a leaf or twig nest beneath it for charm.

I'm deciding the bird should face slightly to one side for personality, and working out a helper function that rotates local coordinates around the Y axis and offsets them from the bird's origin point to position all its parts consistently.

Now I'm planning the capybara's four stubby legs, with front legs slightly longer and hind legs featuring hocks, using inverse kinematics from shoulder/hip points down to small toed feet positioned around the barrel-shaped body.

For feet I'll flatten the sole at ground level with a slightly ellipsoid pad, then add small darker nail capsules at the toe tips—3 for most feet, 4 for front. Now I'm figuring out where the shoulder joint should sit relative to the body's half-width so the leg root attaches naturally inside the torso.

For the front legs, I'm tracing the path from the shoulder pocket down through where it emerges at the body's lower contour, computing the visible leg length and checking it against the chunky leg radius and total reach distance to keep it plausible. Then I do the same calculation for the hind legs, working out hip position, foot placement, and segment lengths so the stride distance stays under the allowed max.

I'm now thinking about adding haunch volumes—round bulges near the hips to give the rump shape—while being careful not to let them poke out past the main body silhouette. For coloring, I'm planning a warm brown-tan capybara coat with countershading (darker back, lighter belly), mottled paint texture, and a scatter of small fur-tuft card elements across the body for texture detail.

For the fur tufts themselves, I'm drawing them as simple tapering blade shapes rendered in grayscale (dark root to light tip), relying on the underlying coat color to tint them rather than baking color into the tuft texture directly. As for whimsical flourishes, I'm leaning toward giving the capybara a tiny bird perched on its head as a playful detail.

Placing the ears on the sides of the skull, flattened ellipsoid shapes with brown outer coloring and darker pink-brown inner coloring, positioned symmetrically near the top of the head.

Defining head geometry constants...

I'm planning the nostrils as small dark angled ellipsoids on the nose bump, then figuring out the mouth: a decal with a philtrum and smile curve placed on the snout's front face, scoped to the area above where the jaw covers the lower face.

Now I'm pinning down the exact snout geometry — frustum coordinates, widths tapering from front to back — so the decal placement aligns correctly with the skull structure underneath.

Now I'm positioning the lower jaw box slightly behind and narrower than the snout, letting it tuck naturally beneath the overhang, then adding a dark mouth decal on the snout's front face with a philtrum line and a curved smile shape to suggest the capybara's mouth.

Projecting the decal onto the snout surface along the direction vector should hit it correctly since the target is restricted to that part. For nostrils, I'm placing small flattened dark ellipsoids near the nose bump center, computing their positions and angles relative to the bump's radii so they sit naturally on the forward-facing surface.

For the eyes, I'm computing positions on the skull sphere using azimuth and elevation angles from its center and radii, placing them in front of the ears at a reasonable height, then sizing the eye decals accordingly.

Now I'm designing the eye texture itself—dark outer ellipse, warmer brown iris ring, pupil, and a highlight dot to give a sleepy, whimsical look within a small viewBox.

I'm adding an upper eyelid shape in coat color with a curved bottom edge, clipped to the eye ellipse so it doesn't bleed outside, plus a thin lid line for definition. For the cheeks, since soft alpha gradients won't survive the cut, I'll use a solid pink ellipse instead for the blush effect.

For a more anime feel, I'm sketching three short pink-red hatch slashes near the cheeks instead of a plain blob, targeting them onto the skull/snout surfaces using the surface selector so they land correctly even with overlapping geometry. Then I'm working out ear placement -- small rounded capybara ears positioned near the top-back of the skull using azimuth/elevation coordinates and a flattened ellipsoid shape.

Still shaping ear geometry...

Maybe I'll treat the ear as a flat extruded outline in the XY plane facing forward, with an inner pink layer offset slightly in front, then tilt the y-axis outward and backward so the ears lean sideways like a real capybara's rather than facing straight ahead.

I need x's sign to flip depending on the side so the ear faces outward correctly: using x:[0,0,-s] makes the thickness point toward +X for the left ear and -X for the right ear, which is what I want.

Now I'm placing the ear against the skull surface, computing where the ellipsoid boundary sits near the top-back sides to find the correct base position and height for the ear outline.

For the bird perched between the ears, I'm sizing it small relative to the capybara's total height and sketching out a whimsical round bird design—thinking teal-blue back, cream belly, yellow beak for a cute finch-like look that contrasts with the capybara's brown tones.

Now I'm working out the bird's construction in local coordinates on top of the skull, defining body ellipsoid dimensions and setting up countershading paint logic so the back reads blue and the belly reads cream based on surface normal direction.

I'm shaping the head as a slightly larger sphere using the same blue countershading, then placing the beak as an orange cone extending forward, with a possible separate lower mandible piece for the jaw joint.

Now I'm defining the skeleton for the bird: a body bone parenting the head, with separate joints for the lower beak, both wings, and the tail. For the face, I'm adding small dark eye spheres with tiny white highlight dots, blush-colored flattened ellipsoids on the cheeks, and teardrop-shaped wing ellipsoids positioned on either side of the body.

Still working out wing orientation...

For the tail I'll use three small flattened feather shapes fanned at slight angles from the base outward. The legs are tiny orange rods running from the belly down to the feet, with the bird perched low so it nestles into the fur rather than standing tall.

Adding three curved crest feathers on the bird's head with varied lean and darker blue coloring with bright tips, plus placing a daisy flower tucked behind the capybara's left ear using a ring of petals facing outward.

I need the petal's flattened dimension to align with the flower's normal direction (the item's local z-axis), giving radii like .007, .014, .003. The flower should sit at the nearest surface point on the skull around azimuth 100°, elevation 40°, with its center offset slightly outward along the normal so it faces away from the skull, and I need to check its placement relative to the ear which sits around az ±100°, x=±.10, z .44.

Checking coordinates more carefully: the eye sits near az 62, el 22, while the ear is closer to az 121, el 50. Placing the daisy around az 95-135, el 28-35 puts it between the eye and ear on top of the head, but I need to verify it doesn't overlap the bird sitting at the center (x within ±.06, z around .5±.065) — nudging the daisy to az 135, el 35 gives safer margins around x=.078, y=.545, z just past .5.

I'm also repositioning the ears themselves, trying az ±140, el 50 versus az ±120, el 38, checking the resulting x/y/z against the bird's body and tail to avoid collisions, since the ear height band (y .57-.65) risks overlapping the tail region near z=.4.

Then I shift to the daisy placement, testing several az/el combinations (88/50, then 100/30) against the wing (outer x ~.07) and eye (x .11, z .56) positions, since each candidate spot keeps clipping into nearby features -- the latest try puts the daisy just below the ear and in front of the eye, but still needs a z-range check against the eye's position.

I decide to make the daisy smaller (petal length ~.014, overall radius ~.024) to give more margin, and settle on separate az angles for the daisy (100) versus the ears (125) to avoid collisions. For the ears, I switch to a more robust approach: using the skin surface hit at az ±128, el 38 to compute the ear base position, then shifting the outline origin slightly inward along the normal.

Now I'm working out the feet and toes for the capybara -- front feet with 4 toes, rear with 3, using small ellipsoids for toes and nails colored darker than the skin, plus starting to pick coat colors.

Writing coat paint logic...

Still writing coat paint function...

Now I'm thinking about adding fur tuft cards as small tapered blade shapes with a gradient from grey root to white tip, tinted by the base coat color so roots read darker. I'll scatter a few hundred of these across the body and sparsely around the cheeks for a ruff effect, skipping the head mostly.

Scattering happens on the body surface with rejection sampling so points don't land inside other meshes, and leg coloring continues to use the same position-based coat paint so the belly and leg undersides read lighter. For the hind haunches, I'm placing ellipsoids near the hip area and need to bind them to the hind leg's first joint so they move naturally with the thigh as it animates.

Now I'm working out the joint chains: hip-knee-ankle for the hind legs and shoulder-elbow-wrist for the front, though since this is a quadruped I'll just classify all four limbs under the same "leg" role rather than distinguishing arm versus leg. I'm mapping out the spine positions from rump to chest and figuring out how the hip and shoulder joints align in z-depth relative to that spine curve.

Writing interpolation helper...

I'm checking proportions now — the chest cap at full radius would extend forward to about z=.54, which overlaps where the head/skull sits around z=.35-.65, so I need to shrink that taper so the torso doesn't collide with the head geometry.

I'm defining the spine chain with four points from hips to chest, then considering adding a short stub tail joint pair hidden near the hips, and a neck joint spanning from chest toward the head base.

Sweeping the neck with a tapered radius for the coat color, then adding head and jaw joints off the neck chain with appropriate offsets and aim directions. I'm now figuring out where the skull center should sit relative to the neck end point.

For the jaw I'm adding a chin ellipsoid and puffy cheek fluff ellipsoids on either side of the lower skull, parented to the head bone for that whimsical capybara look. I'm also planning sparse thin whisker rods from the snout sides, a few per side, using low-poly tube sweeps with tiny radius.

For whimsy I'm adding tiny cream buck teeth as small boxes peeking from beneath the upper lip, positioned to slightly overlap the front of the snout near where the mouth decal ends, parented to the head so they peek out charmingly.

I'm sketching the mouth as a small SVG decal, considering a simple cat-like "w" smile shape built from arcs meeting at a center dip, then curving outward on each side.

Working out the vertical placement of the teeth relative to the snout bottom and jaw front so they hang naturally below the mouth without clipping into the jaw geometry, and positioning the decal box itself around the nose/mouth region accordingly.

Then I turn to blush placement on the cheek fluff surfaces, trying to figure out which parts to target for the surface query and what azimuth/elevation angles from the head center would land the decal correctly on the outermost cheek hit point.

Adding blush decal placement per side with its own offset direction, though I should actually verify this works rather than just reasoning about it — let me check how other sample files handle imports before writing capybara.ts, so I'll peek at the samples directory structure.

input.command: ls; ls samples | head -30; head -20 samples/$(ls samples | head -1); cat package.json | head -30; grep -rn "agentic-3js-builder" tsconfig*.json | head
